title: Fractional Knapsack
directAnswer: You can take fractions of items, so the answer is purely greedy: compute each item's value-to-weight ratio, take items in descending ratio order, and when the next item doesn't fit, take the fraction of it that fills the remaining capacity. Sorting by ratio costs O(n log n); the fill is one linear pass. The fractional twist is exactly what makes greedy optimal here — the 0/1 version (no fractions) is NP-hard and needs DP.

remember.pattern: Sort by value/weight ratio descending, take wholes then one fraction
rules: Sort by the **ratio** value/weight, not by raw value and not by raw weight — both of those lose to ratio on simple counterexamples.
You may take a **fraction** of exactly one item: the last one that partially fits. Every earlier item is taken whole or skipped.
Stop the moment capacity hits 0 — the partial item is always the final action.
Use floating-point (or rational) math for the fractional value; the answer is generally not an integer.
This greedy is optimal **only because fractions are allowed**. If items are all-or-nothing, it's 0/1 Knapsack — a DP problem, not greedy.
whenToUse: Items are divisible — you can take any fraction of an item's weight and earn the same fraction of its value
A single capacity constraint and you want to maximise total value
Continuous resource allocation: fill a budget/bandwidth/volume with divisible goods
You can rank items by a per-unit desirability and greedily consume the best first
antiSignals: Items are indivisible (take all or nothing) → 0/1 Knapsack, solved by DP, not greedy
Multiple capacity dimensions (weight AND volume) → greedy ratio breaks down
Value isn't linear in the fraction taken → the ratio argument no longer holds
You need the actual set of items, not just the max value → still fine, but track choices
remember.takeaway: Fractional Knapsack is the cleanest exchange-argument greedy: per-unit value is the only thing that matters when items split, so always spend remaining capacity on the highest-ratio material left. The single divisibility assumption is the entire difference between an O(n log n) greedy and the NP-hard 0/1 Knapsack — naming that distinction is what interviewers listen for.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you sort by the value/weight RATIO (not raw value or raw weight), realise that divisibility lets exactly one item be split, and can justify the greedy with an exchange argument.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting by highest value or lowest weight instead of best ratio, or forgetting to take the fraction of the last item that only partially fits.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the exchange argument: if any capacity is spent on a lower-ratio item while a higher-ratio item is available, swapping a unit of weight toward the higher ratio strictly increases value — so the optimal solution must be greedy by ratio. Then contrast with 0/1 Knapsack to show you know why fractions matter.

problemStatement:
You are given `n` items, where item `i` has a positive `value[i]` and a positive `weight[i]`, and a knapsack with capacity `W`.

Unlike the classic 0/1 version, you may take **fractions** of items: if you take a fraction `f` (with `0 ≤ f ≤ 1`) of item `i`, you use `f · weight[i]` of capacity and gain `f · value[i]` of value.

Return the ***maximum total value*** you can carry without exceeding the capacity `W`.
constraints: Fractions of items are allowed; the answer may be a non-integer
understanding: Fill a fixed capacity with divisible goods to maximise value. Because any item can be split, the only thing that distinguishes items is value per unit weight. You greedily pour in the densest material first; the very last item you touch is the only one you might take partially, exactly filling the leftover capacity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I take a fraction of an item, or is it all-or-nothing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Fractions are allowed — that's the whole point. If it were all-or-nothing, this would be 0/1 Knapsack and greedy would be wrong; we'd need DP.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the answer be a non-integer?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Taking 2/3 of an item with value 30 contributes 20, so the total is generally fractional. I return a floating-point (or exact rational) value.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are values and weights always positive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Zero or negative weights would let the ratio blow up or go undefined, so I assume strictly positive inputs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if total weight of all items is ≤ W?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then I take everything and return the sum of all values — the loop simply never needs to take a fraction.

examples.explanation: Ratios are 6, 5, 4. Take item0 whole (+60, cap 40), item1 whole (+100, cap 20), then 20/30 of item2 (+120·(20/30)=80). Total 60+100+80 = 240.
Only one item, ratio 16.67. Take 10/30 of it → 500·(1/3) ≈ 166.67.
Everything fits (total weight 15 ≤ 100). Take both whole → 10 + 40 = 50; no fraction needed.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Divisibility is the fork that sends you to greedy instead of DP.

approaches.name: Repeated Max-Ratio Selection (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to lock in the core greedy idea (always take the highest-ratio material) before optimising the selection cost.
hints: Since you can split items, ask: if you had one more unit of capacity, which item would you spend it on? The one with the most value per unit weight.
That suggests always consuming the highest value/weight item available. How do you find it without sorting?
Scan all remaining items each round to find the max ratio, take it (whole or the final fraction), mark it used, and repeat until capacity is 0 or items run out.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each round scans all n items to find the best remaining ratio, and there are up to n rounds → O(n²). No sorting and no extra structure → O(1) extra space beyond a used-marker.
approaches.explanation:
Build the answer by repeatedly grabbing the densest material. Each round, scan every not-yet-taken item, pick the one with the highest `value/weight` ratio, and either take it whole (if it fits the remaining capacity) or take the fraction that exactly fills what's left and stop.

**Why per-unit value is the only thing that matters.** Because items split, a unit of capacity isn't tied to any particular item — you can always spend it on whatever material gives the most value per unit weight. So the decision at every moment is identical: among what's left, which item has the best value/weight? Take from that one. There's no interaction between items beyond competing for the same capacity, which is what makes a one-item-at-a-time greedy correct.

**Why the last item is the only fractional one.** As long as the current best item fits entirely, taking it whole is never worse than taking part of it — you'd just have to fill the rest with something of equal-or-lower ratio. So you take wholes until an item doesn't fit, then take exactly the fraction of that item needed to reach capacity. That single partial take is always the final action.

**Why we don't ship this.** Re-scanning all items every round to find the max ratio is `O(n²)`. The fix is obvious once you see the pattern: the rounds always want items in descending ratio order, so just *sort once* and walk the list. That's the optimal approach.
approaches.insight: The greedy rule itself — 'spend remaining capacity on the highest available value/weight' — is the entire algorithm. The O(n²) here comes only from finding the max by scanning each round; sorting precomputes that order once, which is the single change that makes it fast.

dryRun.intro: Ratios: item0=6, item1=5, item2=4. Each round pick the max-ratio remaining item.

steps.action: scan → max ratio is item0 (6); weight 10 ≤ 50 → take whole
scan remaining → item1 (5); weight 20 ≤ 40 → take whole

java.explanation: Cast to double BEFORE dividing — integer division would truncate the ratio and pick the wrong item.
Item fits entirely → take it whole, no fraction yet.
Doesn't fit → take the fraction that fills the remaining capacity. This is always the last take.

python.explanation: Python 3 `/` is true division, so the ratio is a float automatically.
Partial take: scale the value by the fraction of weight that fits.
Capacity is now full — the loop's guard ends it next iteration.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop guard capacity > 0 is false immediately → returns 0.0.
Every item is taken whole; capacity never forces a fraction, total is the sum of all values.

pitfalls: Integer division when computing the ratio — truncates and silently picks the wrong items.
Sorting by raw value or raw weight instead of the ratio — fails on simple counterexamples.
Skipping this approach as 'too slow to mention' — verbalising the greedy rule first is what the interviewer grades.

approaches.name: Sort by Ratio, One Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'the rounds always want descending ratio order, so sort once and walk'.
hints: The baseline keeps re-finding the highest ratio. What if you arranged the items in that order up front?
Sort items by value/weight descending, then iterate once: take each whole while it fits, and when one doesn't fit, take its fraction and stop.
Sorting is O(n log n); the fill is O(n). The only state you need is the running total and the remaining capacity.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting n items dominates at O(n log n). The fill is a single O(n) pass. Pairing values with weights to sort needs O(n) auxiliary space (or sort index array).
approaches.explanation:
Pair each item's value with its weight, sort the pairs by `value/weight` descending, then sweep once: take each item whole while it fits the remaining capacity; when an item is too big, take exactly the fraction that fills the leftover and stop.

**Why sorting replaces the repeated scan.** The baseline proved the greedy rule is 'always take the highest available ratio'. But that order never changes as items are consumed — the item with the second-best ratio is still second-best after the best is taken. So instead of re-scanning for the max `n` times, sort the items by ratio once and the correct order falls out of the array. That turns `O(n²)` into `O(n log n)`.

**Why a single fractional take is enough.** Walking in descending-ratio order, you take wholes until the running weight would overflow `W`. At that exact item, the leftover capacity `capacity` is less than `weight[i]`, so you take fraction `capacity / weight[i]`, add `value[i] · fraction`, and you're full. Everything before it was strictly higher (or equal) ratio, everything after is lower — so no rearrangement could beat this.

**The exchange argument that proves optimality.** Suppose some optimal solution spends capacity on a lower-ratio item while leaving room it could have given to a higher-ratio item. Move one unit of weight from the lower-ratio item to the higher-ratio one: total value strictly increases (you gain more per unit than you lose), and capacity usage is unchanged. So the original wasn't optimal — contradiction. Repeating this argument shows the optimum must fill capacity in descending ratio order, which is exactly what this algorithm does.

**Why fractions are load-bearing.** This exchange only works because you can move *partial* weight. In the 0/1 version you can't split, so shifting a unit isn't allowed, the argument breaks, and the problem becomes NP-hard. Always say this contrast aloud.
approaches.insight: Sorting is a 'precompute the greedy order once' move. Whenever a baseline repeatedly searches for the current best by a fixed key, sorting by that key collapses the repeated search. The deeper idea is the exchange argument: for a divisible resource, optimal means highest density first, provably.

dryRun.intro: Sort by ratio desc → [(6:w10,v60), (5:w20,v100), (4:w30,v120)]. Walk once.

java.explanation: Sort indices by ratio descending. Comparing b-then-a (not a-then-b) gives the descending order.
W can be up to 10⁹; a long avoids any overflow surprise when subtracting weights.
The single fractional take that exactly fills the remaining capacity, then we stop.

python.line: items = sorted(zip(value, weight), key=lambda vw: vw[0] / vw[1], reverse=True)
python.explanation: Pair each value with its weight and sort by ratio descending in one line.
Whole item fits → take it all and shrink capacity.
Partial take of the boundary item: scale value by the fitting fraction.

diagrams.title: Filling capacity in descending-ratio order
diagrams.caption: Items already sorted by value/weight. The sweep takes wholes, then one fraction. W = 50.

edgeCases.behavior: Every item taken whole; loop ends with capacity > 0 and total = sum of all values.
First (only) item is too big → fractional take W/weight·value.
Order between them doesn't matter; total value is identical either way.

pitfalls: Sorting ascending instead of descending — fills with the worst material first.
Comparing ratios with integer division — truncation reorders items incorrectly.
Forgetting the fractional take and just stopping when an item doesn't fit — leaves capacity unused and undercounts value.

commonMistakes: Sorting by raw value or raw weight instead of the value/weight ratio.
Forgetting to take the fraction of the last item that only partially fits.
Applying this greedy to the 0/1 (indivisible) version, where it's provably wrong.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting by value instead of ratio
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A high-value but heavy item can crowd out two lighter items that together beat it. value=[100,60,60], weight=[50,10,10], W=20: value-first takes part of the 100 (40 value) but ratio-first takes both 60s for 120. Ratio is the only correct key.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: items = sorted(zip(value, weight), key=lambda vw: vw[0], reverse=True)
commonMistakesDetailed.good: items = sorted(zip(value, weight), key=lambda vw: vw[0] / vw[1], reverse=True)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer division corrupts the ratio
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In Java, value[i] / weight[i] with both ints truncates: 60/10 and 100/20 both round oddly relative to each other, scrambling the sort. Cast to double before dividing.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: double ratio = value[i] / weight[i];        // int division, truncated
commonMistakesDetailed.good: double ratio = (double) value[i] / weight[i]; // promote to double first

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dropping the partial item
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Stopping as soon as an item doesn't fit wastes the leftover capacity. The boundary item must be taken fractionally to fill the knapsack completely.

followupVariations.title: 0/1 Knapsack
followupVariations.hint: Items are indivisible — greedy fails; use DP over capacity, O(n·W).

followupVariations.title: Unbounded Knapsack
followupVariations.hint: Indivisible but infinite copies of each item — DP where each item can be reused.

followupVariations.title: Maximum Units on a Truck
followupVariations.hint: Boxes with units per box and a truck capacity — same sort-by-density greedy, but counts are integer (no fractions of a box).

followupVariations.title: IPO (Maximize Capital)
followupVariations.hint: Pick projects under a capital constraint — greedy with a max-heap on profit among affordable projects.

patternNote: Canonical exchange-argument greedy for a divisible resource. Recognise it when items can be split and a single capacity is shared: rank by value-per-unit and consume the densest first. The divisibility assumption is exactly what separates this O(n log n) greedy from the NP-hard 0/1 Knapsack.
